questions.q:
Match each situation (column I) with what the chapter says about it (column II).
Column I: 1. Meena takes two cells out of a wall clock to light a small lamp for her project  2. A board fixed on an electric pole warns passers-by  3. A hill-top windmill turns in the breeze  4. A kitchen wall socket lets a toaster be plugged in
Column II: a. Electricity can be dangerous if not carefully handled  b. Wind energy is being used to generate electricity  c. It delivers supply that reached the house through wires  d. A permitted source for experiments
questions.a: Clock cells are a permitted source; the pole board is a danger sign; the windmill uses wind energy; the socket only delivers supply that came through wires.

questions.q: Sania's torch lamp is dark. She slides the switch to its other position, then back, and goes on sliding, each slide moving the switch to the position it was not in. After 7 slides in all the lamp is ___ (glowing or dark).
questions.a: glowing

questions.q: Nihal's group groups uses by purpose (Lighting, Cooking, ...). Another group suggests grouping by place (home, school, city). Give one example under each place-group and say which grouping makes it easier to spot what work electricity is doing.
questions.a: E.g. home: mixer grinder; school: lights in classrooms; city: street lights. Grouping by purpose shows the work electricity does (light, heat, movement), while grouping by place shows only where it is used.
s: An example under each place-group
Compares what each grouping shows
Gives a reasoned choice

questions.q: A power cut stops the supply that reaches a colony through wires. Four devices are in use: (i) a torchlight with two cells, (ii) a radio plugged into a wall socket, (iii) a wall clock running on a cell, (iv) a mixer grinder plugged into a wall socket. Which pair keeps working?
o: The torchlight and the wall clock
The torchlight and the radio
The wall clock and the mixer grinder
The radio and the mixer grinder
questions.a: The torchlight and the wall clock carry their own portable source (cells). The radio and the mixer grinder as described take the supply that comes through wires to the wall socket, so they stop when it is cut.

questions.q: True or False: A portable generator is a safe source for a school experiment because it is not the wall socket. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says even electricity from portable generators can be dangerous, and that students should use only batteries or cells, like those in torchlights, wall clocks, radios or remotes.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: portable generators can be dangerous; only batteries or cells for experiments

questions.q:
The science club of a school in Ludhiana has six items for its 'Electricity around us' table: a wall clock, a TV remote, a torchlight, a geyser, a mixer grinder and a room heater. The teacher says only some of them can be used for live experiments and the rest must be shown on charts under Nihal's headings.
(a) Which three items can be used for the live experiments, and what common feature allows it?
(b) Under which heading of Nihal's list does each of the other three go?
(c) A parent offers a portable generator so that the geyser and the mixer grinder can also be run live. What does the chapter say, and which items stay the only ones for live use?
(d) The club has time for one display only: a live torchlight demonstration in which visitors open the torch and see the cells, or charts of all six items under Nihal's headings. Choose one and say what the visitors lose.
questions.a: (a) Wall clock, TV remote and torchlight: they run on cells or batteries. (b) Geyser and room heater: Heating and Cooling; mixer grinder: Cooking. (c) Even electricity from portable generators can be dangerous and experiments with power supply must never be performed, so the offer is declined and the same three cell-run items stay. (d) A reasoned choice: the live torchlight lets visitors see the cells, lamp and switch but shows only one device; the charts show the range of six uses but nothing working.
s: Part (a): three cell-run items with the reason
Part (b): correct headings for the other three
Part (c): declines the generator, citing the danger
Part (d): a choice with what is lost

questions.q: A flat has two ceiling fans, a geyser, a refrigerator, a toaster, a television and a water pump, seven devices in all. Using the devices listed under each of Nihal's headings, how many of the seven fall under Heating and Cooling?
o: 4: the two fans, the geyser and the refrigerator
5: the toaster is added because it makes heat
3: the two fans are counted as only one device
6: the television and the pump are added to the four
questions.a: Fans (2), geyser and refrigerator are under Heating and Cooling, so 4. The toaster is under Cooking, the television under Entertainment and the water pump under Others.

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a student breaks the chapter's caution while trying to light a lamp, and then rewrite the situation so that it follows the caution.
questions.a: E.g. Ria plugs a lamp into the lab's wall socket to see how it glows. This breaks the rule never to perform experiments with power supply. Corrected: Ria joins the lamp to two cells taken from a torchlight or wall clock.
s: A situation that uses power supply for an experiment
Names the rule it breaks
Corrected version with cells or batteries

questions.q: Anil asks why the chapter studies electricity through a torchlight instead of a wall-socket device. Give one reason from the chapter's caution and one reason from what a student can actually observe by opening and using a torchlight.
questions.a: Caution: power supply can be dangerous, so experiments use only cells or batteries, and a torchlight runs on cells. Observation: in a torchlight the student can see the lamp, the switch and the cells inside and notice that the lamp glows in only one position of the switch.
s: Caution reason: supply is dangerous, cells or batteries are the permitted source
Observation reason: lamp, switch and cells can be seen and tried

questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's opening.
Statement 1: At a dam, the force of falling water is used to generate electricity, and the supply then reaches towns through wires.
Statement 2: Because a portable generator is small, the chapter permits experiments with it when a teacher is present.
Statement 3: A torchlight is a good starting device because it carries its own portable source of electricity.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 match the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the chapter says even electricity from portable generators can be dangerous and tells students to use only batteries or cells.

questions.q: A student sorts six devices under Nihal's headings: a lift, an immersion rod, a microwave oven, a computer, a radio and an escalator. Place each, and say how many different headings are used.
questions.a: Transportation: lift and escalator. Heating and Cooling: immersion rod. Cooking: microwave oven. Others: computer. Entertainment: radio. Five different headings are used.
s: All six placed correctly
Five headings counted
Lift and escalator share Transportation

questions.q: For a class experiment, four sources are offered: (i) two cells taken out of a wall clock, (ii) a portable generator kept in the school, (iii) cells from a TV remote, (iv) the lab's wall socket with a teacher standing beside it. How many of these does the chapter allow for experiments?
o: Two: the clock cells and the remote cells
Three: the generator is allowed because it is portable
One: only the cells from the wall clock
Four: with a teacher beside it every source is allowed
questions.a: Only (i) and (iii): the chapter says to use only batteries or cells, like those in torchlights, wall clocks, radios or remotes. It says never to experiment with power supply, and even portable generators can be dangerous.

questions.q: The chapter asks learners to suggest other ways of grouping the uses of electricity. (a) Propose one basis for grouping that is not purpose. (b) Place a television, a water pump and an escalator under your groups.
questions.a: E.g. grouping by place of use: television at home, water pump on a farm, escalator in a public place such as a mall or railway station. Any consistent basis with all three devices placed under it earns the marks.
s: Part (a): a valid basis other than purpose
Part (b): all three devices placed consistently

questions.q:
After the Bhakra Nangal trip, Nihal's group builds a presentation on a model town that stands on a windy ridge beside a fast mountain stream. The sun shines most days, and there is no coal or natural gas nearby. Their notes read: (1) falling water is used at the power house; (2) a danger sign stands on a pole outside; (3) wires run from the power house to the town.
(a) Which three ways of generating electricity from the chapter suit this town, and which energy does each use?
(b) Which of the three notes belongs under 'how it reaches us', and what takes the supply to a device inside a house?
(c) The group wants the audience to switch something on. A parent offers a lamp that plugs into the hall's wall socket; the teacher offers a cell-run torchlight. Which must the group use, and what does the danger sign say?
(d) Time allows one demonstration only: the torchlight showing lamp, switch and cells, or a poster of the seven headings of uses. Choose one and say what the audience will miss.
questions.a: (a) Windmills (wind energy), solar panels (the Sun's energy) and falling water (the force of falling water). (b) Note 3, the wires; sockets in the wall take the supply to a device. (c) The torchlight, since only batteries or cells may be used for experiments; the danger sign warns that electricity can be dangerous if not carefully handled. (d) A reasoned choice: the torchlight shows how lamp, switch and cells work together but the audience misses the range of uses; the poster shows the range but not how a device works.
s: Part (a): windmills, solar panels and falling water with their energies
Part (b): wires; sockets take supply to the device
Part (c): torchlight on cells, and what the sign warns
Part (d): a reasoned choice naming what is missed

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A torchlight can be taken apart for a class experiment, but a mixer grinder plugged into a wall socket cannot be used for one.
Reason (R): Electricity from the power supply can be dangerous if not carefully handled, so experiments are to use only cells or batteries.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.a: A is true and R is the chapter's own caution; it is the reason the torchlight (cells) is allowed and the socket-run grinder is not.

questions.q:
Kabir's friend says an escalator in a brightly lit mall belongs under 'Lighting' because the whole mall is lit.
(a) Under which heading of Nihal's list does the escalator belong?
(b) State the rule Kabir can give his friend for choosing a heading for any device.
questions.a: (a) Transportation, with the train, bus, car, scooter and lift. (b) The heading is chosen by what the device does for people (here, carrying them), not by the place where it stands or what else is lit there.
s: Part (a): Transportation
Part (b): heading chosen by what the device does, not where it stands

questions.q: Suppose electricity is cut off in your colony for a whole day. Using the headings of Nihal's list, describe how at least four headings would be affected with one device each, and say which heading you would find hardest to do without. Give a reason.
questions.a: E.g. Lighting: no lights in streets or markets; Cooking: no kettle or mixer grinder; Entertainment: no television or radio; Communication: mobile phones cannot be charged; Heating and Cooling: no fan or refrigerator. A justified choice of the hardest heading (any reasoned answer).
s: Names four headings with an effect on each
Gives a correct device from the chapter for each
Chooses one heading as the hardest
Gives a reason for the choice

questions.q: Sana says, 'My torch lamp glows only when I slide the switch to one position, so the switch must be the source of the electricity.' She opens the torch to test this. Which finding would point to the real source, in keeping with the chapter?
o: Two or more electric cells inside, which are the portable source the torch carries
A lamp inside, because the lamp makes the electricity it uses
A wire running from the switch to a wall socket in the room
The lamp being dark in the other switch position, which proves the switch makes the electricity
questions.a: Inside a torchlight you find two or more electric cells, the portable source. That the lamp glows in only one switch position shows what the switch does, not where the electricity comes from.

questions.q: Divya says, 'A torch cell and a wall socket are both sources of electricity, so a student who may use one may use the other.' Is she correct?
questions.a: No. A cell is a portable source of electricity that students may use for experiments. A wall socket only delivers supply that was generated elsewhere and carried through wires; that supply can be dangerous, so students must never experiment with it.
s: Verdict: not correct
Difference in role: portable source versus a socket delivering supply
Which one students may use and why

questions.q: Differentiate between how electricity is 'generated' and how it is 'supplied', using a hydroelectric power house and a kitchen wall socket as your two examples.
questions.a: At the power house the force of falling water is used to generate electricity. The supply from such sources reaches homes and factories through wires, and the socket in the wall only lets a device be plugged into that supply; it does not generate anything.
s: Generated at the power house by falling water (or another source)
Supplied through wires, with the socket only connecting the device

questions.q: A school can run only one of two displays at its science exhibition. Display 1: a ceiling fan, a mixer grinder and a television connected to the stage socket, which visitors switch on themselves. Display 2: a torchlight, a wall clock and a radio running on cells, open for children to examine, with a poster of Nihal's headings. Judge both displays using the chapter and recommend one, giving two reasons.
questions.a: Display 1 shows the range of devices working, but it means visitors handle power supply, which the chapter says can be dangerous and must never be used for experiments. Display 2 shows less variety of large appliances but uses cells, the permitted source, and lets children see lamp, switch and cells; the poster still shows the range of uses by heading. Recommendation: Display 2, because it follows the caution and because it lets children observe how a device works.
s: Display 1: what it shows and the supply risk
Display 2: what it shows and what it gives up
Compares the two on safety and learning
Recommends Display 2 (or a reasoned choice)
Two reasons from the chapter

questions.q: Nihal's list kept growing as his group moved from home to school to the neighbourhood, the city and the internet. (a) What does the heading 'Others' (water pump, crane, computer) show about the way the group organised its list? (b) A farmer's borewell pump is to be added: under which heading does it go, and why?
questions.a: (a) Some uses did not fit the other headings, so they were placed under Others; the list of uses was long and growing. (b) Others, because it is a water pump, which the list places there.
s: Part (a): some uses fitted no other heading, list kept growing
Part (b): Others, as a water pump

questions.q: A two-cell battery is correctly filled in a holder. Wire X touches the flat disc of the first cell, at the spring end. Wire Y touches the cap of the second cell at the far end. Which statement is correct?
o: Y is the positive terminal of the battery and X is the negative
X is the positive terminal because it is at the spring end
Both wires are positive because both cells are in the holder
Neither can be named without the + and - signs printed on the holder
questions.a: The battery's negative terminal is the disc of the first cell (wire X) and its positive terminal is the cap of the last cell (wire Y). The shape of the ends tells the signs even without printed marks.

questions.q: Differentiate between a 'cell' and a 'battery' as the chapter uses the words, using a three-cell torch and a mobile phone as your two examples.
questions.a: A cell is one source with a positive cap and a negative disc. In a three-cell torch the battery is the three cells joined positive to negative. The chapter notes that the word battery is also used for the single cell that powers a mobile phone.
s: Torch battery: two or more cells joined positive to negative
Single cell also called a battery, as in a phone

questions.q: A two-cell holder has a spring at its left end. Cell A is placed with its flat disc resting on the spring. For the cells to form a battery in the chapter's sense, what must touch the free end of cell A?
o: The flat metal disc of cell B, so cell B has its cap away from cell A
The protruding metal cap of cell B, so cell B has its disc away from cell A
The protruding metal cap of cell B, so both caps touch
Either end of cell B, since cell A is already on the spring
questions.a: Cell A's disc is on the spring, so its free end is the positive cap. The positive terminal of one cell must meet the negative terminal of the next, so the flat disc of cell B touches it.

questions.q:
A torch has three cells in a row, behind the lamp end. Each cell can be placed with its cap towards the lamp or with its flat disc towards the lamp.
(a) In how many different ways can the three cells be placed?
(b) In how many of these ways does an incandescent lamp glow? Explain with the chapter's rule.
(c) The incandescent lamp is replaced by an LED at the lamp end, with its longer wire joined to the lamp end of the battery and its shorter wire to the other end. In how many of the 8 arrangements does the LED glow?
questions.a: (a) 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 ways. (b) Two ways: all three caps towards the lamp, or all three discs towards the lamp, because only then does each positive meet the next negative; an incandescent lamp glows whichever way round the battery is. (c) One way: all caps towards the lamp. Then the lamp end of the battery is positive and meets the LED's longer wire. In the all-discs arrangement the lamp end is negative, so the LED stays dark.
s: Counts 8 arrangements
Finds the 2 working arrangements
Explains with positive-to-negative joins
Incandescent lamp works with either end positive
LED glows in exactly one: all caps towards the lamp

questions.q:
Consider these statements about a torch with three cells in a row.
Statement 1: The lamp glows whichever way round the second cell is placed, as the other two cells fix the order.
Statement 2: If the middle cell of a correctly placed row is turned round, both of its joints become wrong.
Statement 3: The cap of one end cell and the disc of the other end cell are the two ends of the battery when the cells are placed correctly.
Which statements are correct?
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: Statement 1 is false: reversing the second cell spoils the order and the lamp does not glow. Statements 2 and 3 are right: the turned cell has like terminals at both its joints, and the end terminals that are left over are the battery's two terminals.

questions.q:
Navjot's torch has three cells in a row: lamp, cell 1, cell 2, cell 3, spring. After cleaning, she puts them back so that cell 1 and cell 2 both have their metal cap towards the lamp, but cell 3 has its flat disc towards the lamp. The lamp does not glow.
(a) Which two cells are joined wrongly, and which terminals touch there?
(b) How many of the two joints between cells are correct?
(c) What single change will make the lamp glow?
(d) After the repair the torch dims on match day. Her coach says, 'Add a fourth cell next to the lamp and it will surely be brighter.' Where must the new cell's cap and disc go, and how much of the coach's claim does the chapter support?
questions.a: (a) Cells 2 and 3: the flat disc (negative) of cell 2 touches the flat disc (negative) of cell 3. (b) One (the disc of cell 1 touches the cap of cell 2). (c) Turn cell 3 round so its cap is towards the lamp. (d) The new cell's flat disc must touch the cap of cell 1, so its cap is towards the lamp like the others. The chapter says more cells give energy for a longer time and/or more energy, so the claim is only partly supported: it does not promise brighter light.
s: Part (a): cells 2 and 3, negative touching negative
Part (b): one correct joint
Part (c): turn cell 3 round
Part (d): new cell disc to cap of cell 1; claim only partly supported

questions.q: A torch has four cells in a row, all placed correctly, and the lamp glows. Neha takes out the second cell from the lamp end, turns it round and puts it back. How many of the three joints between cells now bring like terminals together?
o: Two, both joints next to the turned cell
One, only the joint nearer the lamp
Three, since one wrong cell upsets every joint
None, as the cell is still in the row
questions.a: The turned cell has a joint with each neighbour. Before, each joint was positive to negative; now both of its joints join like terminals (one negative to negative, the other positive to positive). The joint between the third and fourth cells is untouched.

questions.q: Two cells are placed in a row behind a torch lamp, and each cell may be turned either way. Show that only two of the four possible arrangements can make the lamp glow, and name them.
questions.a: The four arrangements by the part of each cell towards the lamp are: cap, cap; disc, disc; cap, disc; disc, cap. In cap, cap and in disc, disc each cap touches a disc, so the lamp glows. In cap, disc the two discs touch (negative to negative) and in disc, cap the two caps touch (positive to positive), so the lamp stays dark.
s: Lists the four arrangements
Shows cap, cap and disc, disc join positive to negative
Shows the other two join like terminals

questions.q: A row of four cells is correctly placed. (a) How many joints are there between cells? (b) Only the last cell, the one at the spring end, is turned round. How many joints now bring like terminals together, and will the lamp glow?
questions.a: (a) Three joints. (b) One joint (between cells 3 and 4) now joins like terminals; the lamp does not glow because the cells are no longer in the right order.
s: Part (a): three joints
Part (b): one wrong joint and the lamp dark

questions.q:
A school tests a two-cell torch in four trials. The cells sit in a row, lamp then cell 1 then cell 2. Trial 1: both caps towards the lamp. Trial 2: cap of cell 1 towards the lamp, cap of cell 2 away from the lamp. Trial 3: disc of cell 1 towards the lamp, cap of cell 2 towards the lamp. Trial 4: both discs towards the lamp. The torch has an incandescent lamp.
(a) In which trials does the lamp glow?
(b) In each trial where it does not, which terminals touch each other?
(c) The incandescent lamp is replaced by an LED at the lamp end, its longer wire joined to the lamp end of the battery. In which of the four trials does the LED glow?
(d) The teacher must give Class 6 one rule for placing the cells: Rule X, 'put both cells the same way round', or Rule Y, 'put both caps towards the lamp'. Which rule is enough for the incandescent torch, and which for the LED torch?
questions.a: (a) Trials 1 and 4. (b) Trial 2: disc of cell 1 touches disc of cell 2 (negative to negative). Trial 3: cap of cell 1 touches cap of cell 2 (positive to positive). (c) Trial 1 only: only there is the lamp end of the battery positive. In trial 4 the lamp end is negative. (d) Rule X is enough for the incandescent torch (trials 1 and 4 both work). For the LED torch Rule X would allow trial 4, which fails, so Rule Y is needed.
s: Part (a): trials 1 and 4
Part (b): disc-to-disc in trial 2 and cap-to-cap in trial 3
Part (c): LED glows in trial 1 only
Part (d): Rule X for incandescent, Rule Y needed for the LED

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A battery of three cells in a torch can give energy for a longer time and/or more energy than one of its cells.
Reason (R): The three cells of a battery are joined with their positive terminals touching one another.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
questions.a: A is true: connecting more than one cell gives energy for a longer time and/or more energy. R is false: the positive terminal of one cell is joined to the negative terminal of the next.

questions.q: Describe how to place three cells in a row so that exactly one of the two joints is wrong, and say whether the lamp will glow.
questions.a: E.g. place cells 1 and 2 with their caps towards the lamp and turn cell 3 round with its disc towards the lamp. The joint between cells 1 and 2 is correct, but cells 2 and 3 join disc to disc. One wrong joint breaks the order, so the lamp does not glow.
s: A valid arrangement with exactly one wrong joint
Names the like terminals at that joint
Lamp stays dark because the order is broken

questions.q: In a remote, two cells sit side by side. The left cell has its cap upward, and a metal strip at the bottom touches the flat disc of the left cell and also touches the right cell. For the remote to work, which end of the right cell must touch that strip, and how is the right cell therefore placed?
o: Its cap, so the right cell is placed with the cap downward
Its flat disc, so the right cell is placed with the cap upward
Its cap, so both cells are placed with the cap upward
Its flat disc, so the right cell is placed with the cap downward
questions.a: The strip joins the positive terminal of one cell to the negative terminal of the next. It touches the left cell's disc (negative), so it must touch the right cell's cap (positive); the right cell therefore has its cap down.

questions.q: True or False: When three cells are placed correctly in a row, the cap of one end cell and the flat disc of the cell at the other end are the two terminals of the whole battery. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The terminals of the two middle joints are used up, each positive touching a negative, so the only terminals left free are the cap of one end cell and the disc of the other end cell.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the joints use up the terminals in between, leaving one cap and one disc free

questions.q:
Meena's two-cell torch with an incandescent lamp is dark. The lamp glows when tried in another torch, and each cell lights it when joined on its own. Looking inside, she sees the cap of one cell touching the cap of the other.
(a) Name the fault and the terminals that touch.
(b) Why does it stop the lamp?
(c) Give the two single changes that would mend it.
(d) Why does the lamp glow after either change?
(e) Her little brother keeps putting the cells back wrongly. What printed feature of many battery compartments would help him?
questions.a: (a) A positive terminal touches a positive terminal (cap to cap). (b) Cells must be joined with the positive terminal of one to the negative of the next; cap to cap breaks this, so no current flows. (c) Turn either cell round. (d) Each change makes the joint cap to disc, positive to negative, and an incandescent lamp glows whichever end of the battery is positive. (e) The '+' and '-' symbols printed inside the compartment show how to place the cells.
s: Names cap-to-cap, positive to positive
Explains why the order breaks the battery
Two mending changes: turn either cell
Why the incandescent lamp glows either way
Printed + and - symbols as the aid

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Turning one cell round in a working two-cell torch can make the lamp stop glowing.
Reason (R): Connecting more than one cell gives energy for a longer time and/or more energy.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.a: Both are true. A is explained by the positive-to-negative rule of a battery, not by R; R only says why several cells are used.

questions.q: A shopkeeper says, 'Battery always means one cell only.' Is he correct?
questions.a: No. The chapter does say the term battery is also used for a single cell, such as the one in a mobile phone, so he is right that it can mean one cell. But a battery in the main sense is two or more cells connected with the positive terminal of one joined to the negative terminal of the next, as in a torch.
s: Verdict: not correct
Accepts that a single cell is also called a battery
Main sense: two or more cells joined positive to negative

questions.q: A radio has its cells placed side by side in a compartment, each pair of neighbouring cells joined by one metal strip. For a radio that needs 6 cells the number of strips is ___.

A 4-cell torch and a 2-cell torch have the same lamp and all cells are joined correctly. (a) What does the chapter let you say about the 4-cell torch? (b) What single mistake in placing one cell could make the 4-cell torch fail to glow, while the 2-cell torch works?
questions.a: (a) The extra cells provide energy for a longer time and/or more energy. (b) If one of the four cells is turned round, its joints bring like terminals together and the lamp does not glow.
s: Part (a): longer time and/or more energy
Part (b): one cell turned the wrong way breaks the order

questions.q: A three-cell torch is dark. Rita turns only the middle cell round and the lamp glows. Before the change, which joints were wrong, and which terminals touched at each?
questions.a: Both joints beside the middle cell were wrong, because cells 1 and 3 faced one way and cell 2 faced the other. One joint brought the two discs (negative to negative) together and the other brought the two caps (positive to positive) together. Turning cell 2 made both positive to negative, so the lamp glowed.
s: Both joints of the middle cell were wrong
One disc-to-disc and one cap-to-cap
Turning it made every joint positive to negative

questions.q: A working three-cell torch has the metal cap of cell 1 (the cell next to the lamp) pointing towards the lamp. (a) Which way must cells 2 and 3 point? (b) Which part of cell 3 then touches the spring at the far end of the holder?
questions.a: (a) Their caps also point towards the lamp: the disc of cell 1 must touch the cap of cell 2, and the disc of cell 2 the cap of cell 3. (b) The flat metal disc of cell 3 (its negative terminal) rests on the spring.
s: Part (a): caps of cells 2 and 3 towards the lamp, from the positive-to-negative joining
Part (b): flat disc (negative) of cell 3 on the spring

questions.q: A lamp does not glow. You find that the lamp is incandescent, the switch is ON, the cells are in the right order and known to be good, and all wire ends are bare and firmly joined. Which fault remains, and how would you confirm it?
questions.a: The lamp has probably fused, with a broken filament that stops the current. Confirm by looking for the snapped thin wire inside the bulb, or by fitting a lamp known to work in the same circuit.
s: Identifies a fused lamp
Broken filament stops the current
A way to confirm

questions.q: Rahul joins an unlabelled torch lamp to a good two-cell battery and it glows. He then swaps the two wires and it still glows. Which conclusion does the chapter support?
o: It is an incandescent lamp, since an LED would have stayed dark after the swap
It is an LED, since an LED glows whichever way round its wires are joined to the cell
It is a fused lamp, since a fused lamp glows whichever way it is joined to a battery
Nothing can be said, since every torch lamp glows whichever way it is joined to a cell
questions.a: An LED lets current pass in one direction only, so it would be dark in one of the two trials. A lamp that glows both ways is an incandescent lamp. A fused lamp does not glow at all.

questions.q:
Ritvik tests three torch lamps with the same good battery. Lamp P (incandescent) glows with its metal tip on the positive wire, and glows again when he swaps the wires. Lamp Q (an LED) glows with its longer wire on the positive, but not after he swaps. Lamp R (incandescent) does not glow either way; its glass shows a snapped thin wire.
(a) Why did P glow both ways?
(b) Why did Q fail after the swap?
(c) What is the condition of R, and what stops its current?
(d) Ritvik must give lamps to Class 6 children for tomorrow's exhibition, and they often join wires either way round. The store has only LED lamps today; incandescent lamps come next week. Decide between using the LEDs tomorrow with the longer wire marked, or waiting for incandescent lamps, and give one cost of your choice.
questions.a: (a) An incandescent lamp glows whichever terminal joins which, as long as the circuit is complete. (b) Current passes through an LED in one direction only, and after the swap the longer wire met the negative. (c) R has fused: the broken filament stops the current. (d) A reasoned choice. LEDs tomorrow: the exhibition goes ahead, but any child who joins the longer wire to the negative sees no glow, so marking is needed. Waiting: the way of joining cannot stop an incandescent lamp, but the exhibition is delayed and a lamp may fuse.
s: Part (a): either way for incandescent
Part (b): one-direction rule for the LED
Part (c): fused, broken filament
Part (d): a reasoned choice with a cost

questions.q: A torch lamp (incandescent) stays dark although the cells are good, the switch is ON and every connection is firm. Ria has a spare lamp that is known to work. (a) How should she use it to find out whether the lamp or something else is at fault? (b) The spare lamp glows at once. Which part was at fault, and what is the usual cause?
questions.a: (a) Replace the dark lamp by the spare lamp in the same circuit, changing nothing else. (b) The original lamp was at fault; it has fused, usually because its filament is broken.
s: Part (a): swap only the lamp, change nothing else
Part (b): the lamp, fused through a broken filament

questions.q: Write a short set of observations from a student's trial in which she wrongly blames the cell for a dark lamp, and then give the conclusion the observations really support, with the test that shows it.
questions.a: E.g. her incandescent lamp stays dark in both trials, so she says the cell is dead. But the same cell lights another lamp, and the first lamp shows a snapped thin wire. So the lamp has fused and the cell is good; the test is trying the cell on a working lamp, or the lamp in a known good circuit.
s: Observations in which the cell is wrongly blamed
The correct conclusion: lamp fused
A test that separates cell from lamp

questions.q:
Consider these statements about torch lamps.
Statement 1: An LED has no filament, and its two wires are of unequal length.
Statement 2: A fused incandescent lamp stays dark even when its wires are swapped, because the broken filament stops the current.
Statement 3: A good LED that is dark in one way of joining may glow when its wires are interchanged.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: All three agree with the chapter: an LED has no filament and has a longer and a shorter wire; a broken filament stops the current whichever way the lamp is joined; and an LED lets current pass in one direction only.

questions.q: True or False: A torch lamp that stays dark in both trials, one for each way of joining it to a good battery, must be an LED. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. A good LED glows in one of the two ways of joining. A lamp dark in both is a fused incandescent lamp with a broken filament.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: an LED glows in one way; dark both ways means a fused lamp

questions.q:
Four groups tried a lamp with two trials each, joining its wires one way and then the other. All used cells from the same new packet. Group 1 glowed in both trials. Groups 2 and 3 each glowed in one trial only. Group 4 did not glow in either trial, so they blamed their cell. Group 1 then tried Group 4's cell on its own lamp and the lamp glowed. Group 3 noted that in the trial that glowed, the lamp wire joined to the battery's positive was 2.6 cm long and the other was 1.9 cm.
(a) What kind of lamp did Groups 2 and 3 probably have, and what is the clue?
(b) What does Group 1's test tell us about Group 4's problem, and what word describes it for an incandescent lamp?
(c) Does Group 3's note agree with the chapter? What would they see if the 1.9 cm wire were joined to the positive?
(d) Group 2 says, 'Our lamp glowed only once, so it is half fused.' Judge this claim using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) An LED: it glowed in one trial only, which fits current passing in one direction. (b) The cell works, so the fault lies in the lamp, which has probably fused (a broken filament). (c) Yes: the longer wire is the positive terminal and was on the battery's positive. With the 1.9 cm wire on the positive the LED stays dark. (d) Not correct. 'Fused' means a broken filament that stops current in either way; an LED has no filament, and glowing in one way shows the lamp is good.
s: Part (a): LED with the one-direction clue
Part (b): lamp at fault, fused
Part (c): agrees, and dark if the shorter wire is on the positive
Part (d): rejects half fused, LED works in one direction

questions.q: Ishan's torch has an LED lamp and two cells. He takes the battery out and puts it back with its two ends swapped, so the lamp end of the battery is now the other terminal. The lamp stays dark. His brother's torch has an incandescent lamp and the same swap changes nothing. Why the difference?
o: Swapping puts the battery's positive on the LED's shorter wire; an LED passes current one way only
The swap has broken the filament inside the LED, while the filament of the other lamp is stronger
The swap has made the cells in Ishan's torch run out, while the cells in his brother's torch last
An incandescent lamp has no terminals at all, so turning the battery end for end cannot matter to it
questions.a: After the swap the battery's positive terminal meets the LED's shorter wire. An LED works in one direction only, but an incandescent lamp glows whichever of its terminals goes to the positive, so the swap changes nothing there.

questions.q: Differentiate between an incandescent lamp that has fused and a good LED that has been joined the wrong way round, by what is seen in two trials (one each way round), and say which trial result separates them.
questions.a: The fused lamp is dark in both trials. The wrongly joined LED is dark in one trial but glows in the other. Glowing in the second trial is the result that shows it was a good LED.
s: Fused lamp dark in both trials
LED dark in one trial and glowing in the other

questions.q: A box holds three LEDs whose two wires measure (2.4 cm, 1.7 cm), (1.9 cm, 2.6 cm) and (2.2 cm, 1.6 cm). Each LED is joined so that it glows, which means the wire joined to the battery's positive terminal is its longer one. The total length of the wires joined to the battery's positive terminal, over the three LEDs, is ___ cm.

Compare an incandescent lamp and an LED on four points: the filament, which wire or terminal is joined to the battery's positive, what happens when the connection is the wrong way round, and how each could fail to glow though the battery is good. Then justify which of the two you would fit in a torch used by a child who often joins wires carelessly.
questions.a: Filament: present in the incandescent lamp, absent in the LED. Joining: either terminal of the incandescent lamp may go to the positive; the longer (positive) wire of the LED must. Wrong way round: no effect on the incandescent lamp, but the LED stays dark. Failing: the incandescent lamp fails if its filament breaks (fused); the LED fails to glow if joined the wrong way. For the careless child the incandescent lamp suits better, as the way of joining cannot stop it, though it can fuse.
s: Filament comparison
Joining to the positive
Effect of the wrong way round
How each fails to glow
A justified choice for the careless child

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An incandescent lamp whose filament is broken will glow if its two wires are swapped.
Reason (R): A broken filament stops the flow of current.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
questions.a: A is false: with a broken filament the lamp has fused and stays dark whichever way it is joined. R is true; it is the reason the swap cannot help.

questions.q: Three torch lamps are each tried in two trials, one for each way of joining, with a good battery. Lamp P (a thin wire inside the bulb) glows in both trials. Lamp Q (no thin wire) glows in one trial only. Lamp R (a thin wire inside, snapped in two) is dark in both. Which lamp or lamps have fused?
o: R only
Q and R, since each was dark in at least one trial
Q only, since it failed once
P and R, since both have a thin wire inside
questions.a: Fused means a broken filament that stops the current whichever way the lamp is joined. Only R, dark in both trials with a snapped thin wire, has fused. Q is an LED that works in one direction only, and P is a working incandescent lamp.

questions.q: A student records two trials for five lamps (L1 to L5), joining the wires one way in trial 1 and the other way in trial 2. L1: glows, glows. L2: dark, glows. L3: dark, dark. L4: glows, dark. L5: glows, glows. Say which lamps are probably LEDs, which fused, and in which trial the longer wire of L2 and of L4 was joined to the battery's positive.
questions.a: L2 and L4 are LEDs, since each glowed in one trial only. L3 is fused, as it was dark both ways. L1 and L5 are working incandescent lamps. The longer wire of L2 was on the positive in trial 2, and that of L4 in trial 1, the trials in which they glowed.
s: L2 and L4 identified as LEDs
L3 fused, L1 and L5 incandescent
Trial 2 for L2 and trial 1 for L4

questions.q: An LED does not glow in a circuit whose cells are good and whose switch is ON. (a) What cause does the chapter point to? (b) What simple test shows that the LED itself is still good?
questions.a: (a) Its longer (positive) wire is not joined to the positive terminal of the battery, so it is connected the wrong way round. (b) Interchange its two wires; if it now glows, the LED was good.
s: Part (a): joined the wrong way round
Part (b): interchange the wires and see it glow

questions.q: You have three torch lamps without labels, a working incandescent lamp, a fused incandescent lamp and an LED, along with a two-cell battery and wires. Describe how you would tell them apart and what you would see for each.
questions.a: Connect each lamp to the battery. The fused lamp never glows in either way round and may show a snapped filament. The incandescent lamp glows both ways round. The LED glows in only one way round and when its longer wire is on the battery's positive.
s: Connects each lamp to the battery
Fused lamp: no glow either way
Incandescent lamp: glows both ways
LED: glows in one way only
Distinguishes the LED from the fused lamp by trying both ways

questions.q: A class tests 6 incandescent lamps and 4 LEDs, all in working order, with a good battery. Each lamp is tried in two trials, one for each way of joining its wires. (a) In how many of the 20 trials does the lamp glow? (b) In how many is it dark, and which lamps give those dark trials?
questions.a: (a) 6 x 2 = 12 trials with incandescent lamps glow, and each of the 4 LEDs glows in one trial, so 12 + 4 = 16 trials. (b) 4 trials are dark, one for each LED, in the way its longer wire meets the negative terminal.
s: Part (a): 16 glowing trials
Part (b): 4 dark trials, all LEDs

questions.q: Dev says, 'My torch has an LED and I put in two cells instead of one, so more energy flows and the LED will now glow whichever way round I join it.' Is he correct?
questions.a: No. Connecting more cells gives energy for a longer time and/or more energy, but it does not change the rule for an LED. Current passes through an LED in one direction only, so its longer wire must still be joined to the positive terminal of the battery.
s: Verdict: not correct
More cells give longer time and/or more energy only
LED still needs the longer wire to the positive terminal

questions.q: Priya's friend says, 'My LED did not glow when I joined it to the battery, so it has fused.' Why is the word 'fused' a poor description in the chapter's terms, and what should she try first?
o: An LED has no filament to break, so she should first join its wires the other way round
An LED has a hidden filament, so she should look for the snapped thin wire inside the LED bulb
An LED can fuse only when its battery has two cells, so she should take one of the cells out
An LED fuses whenever it stays dark in a circuit, so she should replace it with a new LED
questions.a: The chapter uses 'fused' for an incandescent lamp whose filament is broken. An LED has no filament, and it also glows only when its longer wire meets the battery's positive, so the first thing to try is interchanging its wires.

questions.q:
Match each set-up (column I) with the result the chapter predicts (column II).
Column I: 1. An incandescent lamp whose metal tip is joined to the battery's negative terminal  2. An LED whose longer wire is joined to the battery's negative terminal  3. An incandescent lamp with a snapped thin wire, joined to a good battery  4. An LED whose longer wire is joined to the battery's positive terminal
Column II: a. Glows, as either terminal of the lamp may go to the positive  b. Stays dark, as current passes through an LED in one direction only  c. Stays dark whichever way it is joined, as it has fused  d. Glows, as the positive terminal of the LED meets the positive of the battery
questions.a: The incandescent lamp glows either way; the wrongly joined LED stays dark; the snapped filament means a fused lamp; the correctly joined LED glows.

questions.q: Vidyut's circuit has a cell, a switch in the ON position and an incandescent lamp, yet the lamp does not glow. (a) Give two possible reasons, one about the path and one about a component. (b) Describe one way to find out which of your reasons is the real one.
questions.a: (a) Path: a wire end is loose or still covered, so the path is not complete. Component: the lamp has fused (broken filament) or the cell is not working. (b) Replace the lamp by one known to work in the same circuit, or test the cell with a lamp that works; if the lamp then glows, the part you replaced was at fault.
s: Part (a): one path reason and one component reason
Part (b): replace one part by a known good one and observe

questions.q: Meera has a cell, a lamp and two wires. Wire 1 joins the lamp's metal case to the cell's protruding cap. Wire 2 joins the lamp's metal tip to the same cap. Nothing is joined to the flat disc of the cell, and her friend says, 'Both lamp terminals are connected to the cell, so it must glow.' Why does the lamp stay dark?
o: Both lamp terminals reach only the positive terminal and nothing reaches the negative one
Wire 2 should have been joined to the lamp's metal case instead of to the lamp's metal tip
The cell has to be turned round so that its flat disc faces the lamp and its cap faces away
A lamp glows only when it is joined to a battery of two cells and never to a single cell
questions.a: A circuit needs one terminal of the lamp joined to one terminal of the cell and the other terminal of the lamp to the other terminal of the cell. Here the negative terminal is left out, so no current flows round.

questions.q: Describe a circuit built from a good cell, a good lamp, a switch in the ON position and wires with no loose end, in which the lamp still does not glow. Give the reason in terms of the path, and say how to mend it.
questions.a: E.g. both wires of the lamp are joined to the same terminal of the cell. There is then no path from one terminal of the cell through the lamp to the other terminal, so the circuit is not complete. Move one lamp wire to the other terminal of the cell.
s: A valid circuit with the lamp dark
Reason: no complete path
The mend

questions.q: In a circuit with a cell, a lamp and a safety-pin switch, the lamp is dark with the pin touching both drawing pins. Ritu fits a lamp known to work, and it is still dark. She puts the original lamp back and fits a new cell, and the lamp glows. Which part was at fault?
o: The original cell
The original lamp
The safety-pin switch
One of the wires
questions.a: The known-good lamp was dark, so the lamp was not the only reason. With the original lamp back and only the cell changed, the lamp glows, so the first cell was not working. The switch and wires stayed the same and the circuit worked.

questions.q:
Ishaan builds four circuits with the same cell, the same lamp and a safety-pin switch. Attempt 1: the two lamp terminals are joined by wires to the two terminals of the cell, and the switch is ON. Attempt 2: built the next day, the switch looks ON, but the lamp stays dark. Attempt 3: both wires of the lamp are joined to the positive terminal of the cell, switch ON. Attempt 4: the lamp is joined correctly and the switch is on the wire between the lamp and the negative terminal, switch ON.
(a) Of attempts 1, 3 and 4, in which does the lamp glow?
(b) Explain attempt 3.
(c) Which one wire of attempt 3 would you move, and to where, to make the lamp glow?
(d) A friend says attempt 2's cell must be faulty. Using the other attempts, say whether she is supported, and name the first check you would make, with the reason for your order.
questions.a: (a) Attempts 1 and 4. (b) Both lamp wires go to the same terminal, so there is no complete path through the lamp from one terminal of the cell to the other. (c) Move one lamp wire to the negative terminal of the cell. (d) Not supported: the same cell lit the same lamp in attempts 1 and 4. The first check is the switch contact (the pin may not rest firmly on both drawing pins, though it looks ON), then the wire ends and the lamp; replace the cell last.
s: Part (a): attempts 1 and 4
Part (b): no complete path
Part (c): move one lamp wire to the negative terminal
Part (d): the cell is not suspect, switch contact first, with a reason for the order

questions.q: A cell's cap is joined by a wire to the metal tip of a lamp. The lamp's metal case is joined to one drawing pin of a safety-pin switch, and the other drawing pin is joined to the cell's flat disc. (a) With the switch ON, write the order of the parts the current is taken to pass through, starting from the cap. (b) At which place does the path stop when the safety pin is lifted away?
questions.a: (a) Cap, wire, lamp tip, filament, lamp case, wire, first drawing pin, safety pin, second drawing pin, wire, disc. (b) At the gap between the free end of the safety pin and the second drawing pin.
s: Part (a): cap, through the lamp and the closed switch, to the disc
Part (b): the gap at the second drawing pin

questions.q:
Consider these statements about a circuit with a cell, a lamp and a safety-pin switch.
Statement 1: A switch placed on the wire between the lamp and the negative terminal of the cell can still turn the lamp on and off.
Statement 2: In a closed circuit the current is taken to leave the cell from its protruding cap.
Statement 3: When the safety pin touches only one drawing pin, the lamp still glows because the cell and the lamp are good.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, and the cap is the positive terminal from which the current is taken to leave. Statement 3 is false: the gap leaves the circuit open, whatever the state of the cell and lamp.

questions.q: A student wrote these steps for making a switch: 'Push a drawing pin through the ring of the safety pin so that it cannot move. Fix the second drawing pin far away from the pin. Join one wire to the first drawing pin and nothing to the second. The lamp glows when the pin does not touch the second drawing pin.' Find and correct the four errors, and explain why the lamp glows only when the corrected switch is in the ON position.
questions.a: The safety pin must be able to rotate freely. The second drawing pin must be fixed so that the free end of the safety pin can touch it. A wire must be joined to each drawing pin. The lamp glows when the pin touches the second drawing pin. It glows only then because touching both pins closes the gap, completes the path and lets the current flow; otherwise the circuit is open.
s: Pin must rotate freely
Second pin placed so the free end can touch it
A wire to each drawing pin
Lamp glows when the pin touches both pins
Explains the closed gap and complete path

questions.q: Differentiate between the roles of the cell and the switch in a torch by saying what you would see if (i) the switch were replaced by a continuous wire and (ii) the cell were taken out.
questions.a: (i) With a continuous wire in place of the switch, the circuit would always be closed, so the lamp would glow all the time and could not be turned off. (ii) Without the cell there is no source of electrical energy, so the lamp would never glow whatever the switch does.
s: Part (i): lamp always on, cannot be switched off
Part (ii): no source so the lamp never glows

questions.q: In a closed circuit a two-cell battery lights an LED, with a switch in the ON position. Following the chapter's convention for the direction of current, through which part does current enter the LED?
o: Through its longer wire, the one joined towards the battery's positive terminal
Through its shorter wire, the one joined towards the battery's negative terminal
Through both wires at the same time
It enters through neither, as an LED works without current
questions.a: Current is taken to flow from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell, and an LED glows only when its longer (positive) wire is joined towards the battery's positive terminal. So the current enters by the longer wire.

questions.q: A single loop contains a cell, a lamp and two safety-pin switches. Show that the lamp cannot glow if either switch is in the OFF position, however the other is set.
questions.a: In the loop the current has only one path and must pass through every part of it. A switch in the OFF position leaves a gap, so the circuit is open there. With no complete path no current flows, and the lamp does not glow, whatever the other switch is doing.
s: The single loop gives one path through every part
An OFF switch leaves a gap and opens the circuit
No complete path means no current and no glow

questions.q:
A vendor at a market stall has a lamp over his name board, run from a box of cells, that glows when its switch is ON. One evening it does not glow with the switch ON and a fresh set of cells. The electrician says the path is broken somewhere. He finds a loose wire end under the switch, tightens it, and the lamp glows. The vendor wants the switch at his counter, 3 m from the lamp, which needs extra wire. The alternative is a switch fixed right beside the lamp, which needs a ladder to reach.
(a) What kind of circuit was it before the repair, and which switch position does it resemble?
(b) Name two places in the circuit where such a break could be, using only parts named in the chapter.
(c) In the working circuit, from which terminal of the cell to which is the current taken to flow?
(d) Which switch position would you advise, and what is one drawback of your choice?
questions.a: (a) An open circuit; it resembles the OFF position. (b) Any two: a loose wire end, the switch, the lamp's connections, the cell's connections. (c) From the positive terminal to the negative terminal. (d) A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, so the counter is possible; drawback: extra wire gives more joints that may come loose. The switch beside the lamp needs a ladder every time. Either choice with a reasoned drawback.
s: Part (a): open circuit, like OFF
Part (b): two valid places in the circuit
Part (c): positive to negative
Part (d): reasoned choice with a drawback

questions.q: A single loop has a cell, a lamp and two safety-pin switches, S1 near the cell and S2 near the lamp, with nothing else in the loop. In which positions of the two switches does the lamp glow?
o: Only when both switches are ON
When either switch is ON
Only when exactly one switch is ON
Whatever the positions, as long as the cell is good
questions.a: The loop gives current only one path, so every part of it, including both switches, must be closed. If either switch is OFF there is a gap and the circuit is open.

questions.q: Ayaan tries four things one at a time on a dark lamp circuit: (i) he makes sure the switch is ON, (ii) he presses every wire end firmly, (iii) he fits a lamp known to work, (iv) he fits a new cell. The lamp glows after step (iii). (a) Which part was at fault? (b) What do steps (i) and (ii) show about the path before the repair?
questions.a: (a) The original lamp, which had probably fused. (b) The switch was already closed and the wire ends were already firm, so the path was complete and the lamp was the only reason for no current through it.
s: Part (a): the original lamp
Part (b): the path was already complete

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Moving the switch from beside the cell to beside the lamp does not change whether the lamp can be turned on and off.
Reason (R): The direction of electric current in a circuit is taken to be from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.a: Both are true. A holds because a switch only completes or breaks the one path; the convention for the direction of current has nothing to do with where the switch sits.

questions.q: Anita draws a circuit in which a cell's cap is on the left, a switch is ON, and a lamp is on the right. She marks arrows showing the current going from the flat disc, through the lamp, to the cap. (i) Is she right? (ii) Give the correct direction. (iii) Would the direction change if she replaced the lamp by a different working lamp?
questions.a: (i) No; she has drawn the arrows the wrong way. (ii) The current is taken to flow from the positive terminal (the cap), through the switch and lamp, to the negative terminal (the disc). (iii) No; the direction depends on the cell's terminals and stays the same for any lamp.
s: The arrows are the wrong way
Correct direction: cap through the lamp to the disc
The direction does not depend on the lamp

questions.q: A torch does not work. Write four checks, in a sensible order, using ideas from this chapter. Say what each check looks for, and what the common cause of all the faults is.
questions.a: Check the switch is in the ON position (a gap keeps the circuit open); check the cells are in the right order, positive to negative; check the lamp for a broken filament (fused), or an LED for the right direction; check that the connections touch and are complete. Whichever fault is found, the cause is that the path is incomplete or the current cannot pass.
s: Check of the switch position
Check of the cell order
Check of the lamp filament or LED direction
Check of the connections
Conclusion linked to a complete path

questions.q: Pooja makes a switch from two drawing pins and a safety pin on cardboard, but she fixes the second drawing pin so far from the first that the free end of the safety pin cannot reach it. She joins a wire to each pin and puts the switch in a circuit with a good cell and lamp. What happens?
o: The switch can never close, so the lamp stays dark in every position of the pin
The lamp glows only when the pin is rotated away from both of the drawing pins
The lamp always glows because the safety pin touches the first of the drawing pins
The lamp glows dimly in every position because the circuit is only half closed
questions.a: The switch closes only when the safety pin touches both drawing pins. Here the free end can never touch the second pin, so the gap stays and the circuit is always open.

questions.q: True or False: In a circuit with an incandescent lamp, which glows whichever way round it is joined, the current is still taken to flow from the positive terminal of the cell, through the lamp, to the negative terminal. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: True. The direction of current in a circuit is taken to be from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell. That an incandescent lamp glows whichever of its terminals goes to the positive does not change this convention.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the convention depends on the cell's terminals, not on the lamp's

questions.q: Imran says, 'Every wire in my circuit is joined firmly and the switch is ON, so the lamp must glow.' Is he correct?
questions.a: No. Firm wires and an ON switch are not enough. The wires must form a complete path from one terminal of the cell through the lamp to the other terminal, and the parts must work. For example, both lamp wires may go to one terminal of the cell, or the lamp may have fused, so the lamp can stay dark.
s: Verdict: not correct
A path fault, such as both wires on one terminal
A component fault, such as a fused lamp

questions.q:
Match each fault found in a dark-lamp circuit (column I) with the repair that fixes it (column II).
Column I: 1. The switch is ON, but one wire end is only lying near the cell terminal  2. The safety pin touches only one drawing pin  3. Every connection is firm and the switch is ON, but the thin wire inside an incandescent lamp has snapped  4. The wire ends are still wrapped in plastic
Column II: a. Press the wire end firmly on the terminal to complete the path  b. Rotate the pin until it touches the second drawing pin  c. Fit a lamp that is known to work  d. Remove about 1 cm of the covering to expose the metal
questions.a: A loose wire end needs pressing on; a switch pin needs to close the gap; a snapped filament needs a new lamp; covered wire ends need about 1 cm of covering removed.

questions.q:
Consider these statements about circuit diagrams.
Statement 1: A switch symbol drawn with a gap shows the switch in the ON position.
Statement 2: In the symbol of an LED, the triangle points in the direction in which current can flow.
Statement 3: The long line of a cell symbol is its negative terminal.
Which statements are correct?
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: Only Statement 2 is correct: the triangle points the way current can flow. A gap shows the OFF position, not ON, and the long line of a cell symbol is the positive terminal.

questions.q: In a diagram, a wire runs from the long line of a cell symbol to a switch symbol drawn closed, then to the base of an LED triangle; from the tip a wire goes back to the short line of the same cell. Write the order in which you meet the symbols going from the long line, say where you finish, and give the direction of the current in the real circuit.
questions.a: The order is: long line (positive terminal), switch, base of the LED triangle, tip of the triangle, short line. You finish at the cell's negative terminal. The current is taken to flow from the positive to the negative terminal, so it goes the same way round as you traced, and enters the LED at its base.
s: Order of the symbols
Finish at the negative terminal
Direction of current is the way traced, positive to negative

questions.q: Isha draws a cell symbol with one long and one short line and joins an LED symbol to it so that the LED can glow. Since the triangle of the LED symbol points the way current can flow, its flat base must be joined towards the ___ line of the cell symbol.
questions.a: long

questions.q: A teacher in Pune draws a torch circuit with the standard symbols, and an engineer in Japan reads it without any help. Explain why this is possible, and name one body that creates such symbols.
questions.a: Standard symbols are the same across the world, so people from different countries and industries understand each other easily. Bodies that create them include the IEC, ANSI and IEEE (any one).
s: Same standard symbols used across countries
Names one of IEC, ANSI or IEEE

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A circuit diagram in which the switch symbol is drawn with a gap shows a lamp that does not glow.
Reason (R): A switch symbol drawn with a gap means the switch is in the ON position.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
questions.a: A is true: the gap means the circuit is open. R is false: a gap means the OFF position; the ON position is drawn closed.

questions.q:
Four students draw circuits with cells, a lamp or an LED, and a switch. Diagram A: one cell, a lamp symbol and a switch drawn closed in one loop. Diagram B: two cells joined long line to short line, an LED whose triangle points from the positive end to the negative end, and a switch drawn with a gap. Diagram C: two cells joined long line to short line, a switch drawn closed, and an LED whose triangle points from the negative end to the positive end. Diagram D: two cells joined short line to short line, a switch drawn closed and an LED whose triangle points from the positive end to the negative end.
(a) For each of A, B, C and D, say whether the real lamp would glow and give the reason.
(b) Which one of the dark circuits would glow if only its switch symbol were redrawn?
questions.a: (a) A glows: complete loop, switch closed. B is dark: the gap means the switch is OFF and the circuit is open. C is dark: the triangle points the wrong way, so the LED lets no current through. D is dark: the cells are joined short line to short line, negative to negative, so they do not form a working battery. (b) B only; its cells and LED are right, and closing the switch completes the circuit.
s: Diagram A glows with the reason
Diagram B dark because of the gap
Diagram C dark because of the reversed triangle
Diagram D dark because of the cell joining
B is the one that glows if only the switch is redrawn

questions.q: A diagram shows a cell symbol, a lamp symbol and a switch symbol drawn with a gap, all in one loop. (a) What does the gap tell you about the real circuit? (b) Rani redraws the same parts with the switch symbol on the other side of the lamp. Has the lamp's behaviour changed? Why?
questions.a: (a) The switch is OFF, so the circuit is open and the lamp does not glow. (b) No. A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit, and the gap still leaves the loop open, so the lamp stays dark.
s: Part (a): OFF, open circuit, no glow
Part (b): no change, the gap still opens the loop

questions.q: Isha says, 'If a diagram shows two cell symbols with the long line of one joined to the short line of the next, the two cells form a battery.' Is she correct?
questions.a: Yes. The long line is the positive terminal and the short line the negative, so this joins the positive of one cell to the negative of the next, which is how cells are connected to make a battery.
s: Verdict: correct
Long line positive, short line negative
Positive to negative joining makes a battery

questions.q: Diagram X shows two cell symbols in a row, each drawn long line then short line from left to right. The long line at the left end is joined to the base of an LED triangle, the tip is joined through a switch symbol drawn closed to the short line at the right end. Diagram Y is the same except that the second cell symbol is drawn short line then long line. In which diagram do the chapter's rules let the LED glow?
o: Only X, as Y joins the short line of one cell to the short line of the next
Only Y, as Y has a long line at the far right end of the battery drawing
Both, as the switch symbol is drawn closed in each of the two drawings
Neither, as an LED symbol cannot be drawn together with two cell symbols
questions.a: In X every short line (negative) meets a long line (positive), so the cells form a battery with its positive end at the left, joined to the triangle's base. In Y two short lines meet, which is negative to negative, so there is no working battery.

questions.q:
In a Class 7 test, Meghna draws the circuit of a torch whose real battery has its positive terminal at the left end. Her cell symbol has the long line on the left and the short line on the right. The base of her LED triangle is joined to the short line, the tip is joined through a switch symbol drawn closed to the long line. Her teacher says the diagram would be right if she changed just one thing.
(a) Which end of her cell symbol is the positive terminal?
(b) Why would the LED not glow in a real circuit built as drawn?
(c) Name the two single changes that would give a diagram in which the LED can glow.
(d) Which of the two changes shows her real torch faithfully, and why?
questions.a: (a) The left end, the long line. (b) The base of the triangle is joined to the negative end and the tip to the positive end, so the triangle points against the direction in which current is taken to flow, and an LED lets current pass in one direction only. (c) Turn the LED symbol round, or redraw the cell with the long line on the right. (d) Turning the LED symbol round, because the real battery has its positive terminal at the left; moving the long line to the right would show the wrong end of the real battery as positive.
s: Part (a): the long line on the left
Part (b): triangle points against the current
Part (c): two changes: turn the LED, or swap the cell's lines
Part (d): turning the LED, because the real positive end is on the left

questions.q: True or False: The two arrows in the symbol of an LED show the direction in which the current can flow through it. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The two arrows show that the LED emits light; it is the triangle that points in the direction in which current can flow.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: arrows mean light is emitted, the triangle shows the direction of current

questions.q: A student wrote about her diagram: 'The long line of the cell symbol is the negative terminal. The switch symbol drawn with a gap shows the circuit is closed. Every country draws its own symbols, so my diagram cannot be read abroad. I made a battery by joining two cell symbols long line to long line.' Find and correct the four errors, and say which one of the four, if built in a real circuit, would stop the lamp glowing even with the switch ON.
questions.a: The long line is the positive terminal. A gap means the switch is OFF and the circuit open. The symbols are standard (IEC, ANSI, IEEE), so a diagram can be read abroad. Cells joined long line to long line bring positive to positive; a battery joins long line (positive) to short line (negative). The last error is the one that would stop a real lamp even with the switch ON, since the cells are not joined as a battery.
s: Long line is positive
Gap means OFF and open
Symbols are standard across countries
Battery is joined long line to short line
Identifies the cell-joining error as the one that stops the lamp

questions.q: The circuit of a torch is drawn with a cell symbol, a lamp symbol and a switch symbol drawn with a gap, all in one loop. Which single change to the drawing shows a lamp that glows?
o: Redrawing the switch symbol without the gap, in the ON position
Moving the lamp symbol to the other side of the cell symbol in the loop
Drawing the wires longer so that the symbols are farther apart in the loop
Swapping the long and the short lines of the cell symbol in the drawing
questions.a: The gap shows an open circuit. Only closing the switch symbol completes the loop. Moving the lamp, lengthening the wires or swapping the cell's lines leaves the gap in place.

questions.q: Describe a diagram of an LED circuit with a two-cell battery in which the LED would stay dark only because one symbol is drawn the wrong way round. Say which symbol, and how to correct it.
questions.a: E.g. the two cells are joined long line to short line and the switch is drawn closed, but the triangle of the LED symbol points from the negative end of the battery to the positive end. The LED symbol is the one wrong; turn it round so that the triangle points from the positive end to the negative end.
s: A diagram with exactly one reversed symbol
Names the symbol that is wrong
The correction

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the symbol of an LED the two arrows cannot be used to decide how the LED is connected to a battery.
Reason (R): The arrows show that the LED emits light, while the triangle shows the direction in which current can flow.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.a: The arrows only say that the LED gives out light, so the connection must be decided from the triangle. Both statements are true and R explains A.

questions.q: A battery is drawn as four cell symbols in a row, each with its long line on the left and short line on the right. The number of places in the drawing where the short line of one cell meets the long line of the next is ___.

The science club draws the circuit of a night-light for a notice board. It has a battery of three cells, a switch and one LED. Drawing X: three cell symbols in a row, each drawn long line then short line from left to right, the long line at the left end joined through a switch symbol drawn closed to the base of the LED triangle, and the tip of the triangle joined to the short line at the right end. Drawing Y: the same, except that the middle cell symbol is drawn short line then long line.
(a) At how many joints between cells does a long line meet a short line in X, and in Y?
(b) Which drawing allows the LED to glow, and which end of the battery is positive in it?
(c) If X is redrawn as its mirror image, with every cell symbol drawn short line then long line, to which end must the base of the LED triangle be joined?
(d) The board has room for only one drawing. A teacher says showing Y with a note would teach more than X alone. Decide, and say what the note on Y must say.
questions.a: (a) X: 2 joints; Y: 0 joints (the first joint is short to short and the second long to long). (b) X; the left end (the long line) is positive. (c) To the right end, which is then the long line and so the positive end. (d) A reasoned choice. Y with a note shows a common mistake; X alone shows only the correct pattern. The note must say that Y joins like terminals (short to short, then long to long, negative to negative and positive to positive), so it is not a working battery, and that the middle cell must be turned round.
s: Part (a): 2 joints in X and 0 in Y
Part (b): X, with the left end positive
Part (c): the right end, as it is now the long line
Part (d): a reasoned choice with the content of the note

questions.q: A battery of three cells is drawn as three cell symbols in a row, each with its long line first (on the left). (a) How many long lines and how many short lines does the whole drawing have? (b) Which end line of the drawing is the positive terminal of the battery, and which is the negative?
questions.a: (a) 3 long lines and 3 short lines, 6 lines in all. (b) The long line at the left end is the positive terminal and the short line at the right end is the negative terminal; the lines in between meet long to short.
s: Part (a): 3 long and 3 short
Part (b): left end positive, right end negative

questions.q: Between an incandescent lamp and an LED, which one needs its circuit symbol to carry a direction, and why?
questions.a: The LED. Current can pass through an LED in one direction only, so its symbol has a triangle pointing the way current can flow. An incandescent lamp glows whichever way it is connected, so no direction is needed.
s: Names the LED
Gives the one-direction reason against the incandescent lamp working either way

questions.q: In a drawing, two cell symbols in a row are each drawn short line then long line from left to right. The base of an LED triangle is joined to the far right end of the battery, and the tip is joined through a switch symbol drawn closed to the far left end. Anil says the LED cannot glow because the long line must be on the left. Who is right?
o: The LED glows: the right end is a long line (positive) and the base is joined to it
Anil is right: a battery is read correctly only when its long line is at the left
The LED glows only if the switch symbol is drawn with a gap between its parts
The LED cannot glow because the base of the triangle must touch a short line
questions.a: Which end is positive depends on the line lengths, not on the side of the page. The two cells join long line to short line, the right end is a long line (positive) and the triangle's base is joined to it, so the LED glows.

questions.q: A student draws a circuit of a three-cell battery, one LED and one switch, with the cells correct. She tries every drawing in which the LED triangle points one way or the other round the loop and the switch is drawn ON or OFF. How many drawings is that, and in how many can the LED glow? Give the reason.
questions.a: 2 directions of the triangle x 2 switch states = 4 drawings. Only one can glow: the triangle pointing from the positive end to the negative end with the switch drawn ON. A reversed triangle stops current in an LED, and a switch drawn with a gap leaves the circuit open.
s: Counts 4 drawings
Identifies the 1 that can glow
Reasons for the other three

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The top of an electric plug is covered with an insulator such as plastic.
Reason (R): Copper is mainly used for electrical wires because of its comparatively lower cost and abundant supply.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.a: Both are true, but the cost and supply of copper has nothing to do with covering the plug top; the cover is there to protect people from electric shocks.

questions.q: Show that a plug made entirely of conductors cannot be a good plug, and that a plug made entirely of insulators cannot be one either.
questions.a: A plug made entirely of conductors would pass current to the appliance, but its top would conduct to a person's hand and could give an electric shock, as the body is a conductor. A plug made entirely of insulators would be safe to hold, but its connectors would not let current pass, so the appliance would not work. A good plug needs conducting connectors and an insulating top.
s: All-conductor plug works but gives shocks
All-insulator plug is safe but cannot pass current
A good plug needs both
