questions.q: Priya tests eight objects one by one with a conduction tester whose free ends are kept apart: a steel key, a metal coin, a copper wire, aluminium foil, an iron pin, a plastic ruler, a rubber eraser and a ceramic cup. The number of objects for which the lamp stays dark is ___.
True or False: A wall clock that runs on a cell uses Alternating Current, whereas a mixer grinder plugged into a wall socket uses Direct Current. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The two are the wrong way round. Cells and batteries usually power small devices with Direct Current, while the electricity from power plants that reaches the wall socket is Alternating Current and can run larger appliances.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the clock on a cell uses DC and the mixer on the wall socket uses AC

questions.q: Priya puts a switch in her conduction tester, in the OFF position, and touches the free ends to a steel key. The lamp stays dark. She writes, 'Steel key: insulator.' What is wrong with her conclusion?
o: The switch is OFF, so the circuit is open and the lamp would stay dark for any object
A steel key conducts only when it is wet, so a dry key always keeps the lamp dark
A key made of metal always lights the lamp at once, even with the switch in OFF
A switch cannot be added to a tester without changing the cell that it uses
questions.a: With the switch OFF there is a gap, so no current flows whatever the object is. The dark lamp therefore says nothing about the key; she should close the switch first.

questions.q: Four plug designs are proposed for a school model. Design M: metal connectors and a plastic top. Design N: plastic connectors and a metal top. Design P: metal connectors with the metal top left bare. Design Q: ceramic connectors and a rubber top. Using the chapter, say for each design whether current reaches the appliance and whether it is safe to hold, and decide which design is acceptable. Name one caution about using a plug at home.
questions.a: M: current passes through the metal connectors and the plastic top insulates, so it works and is safe. N: plastic connectors do not let current pass, so it fails, and the bare metal top could give a shock. P: the connectors pass current, but the bare metal top can give an electric shock, so it works but is unsafe. Q: ceramics and rubber are insulators, so it is safe but no current passes. Only M is acceptable. Caution: never touch plugs with wet hands, or use a plug that is broken or has damaged insulation.
s: Design M works and is safe
Design N fails and is unsafe
Design P works but is unsafe
Design Q is safe but does not work
Chooses M and gives a correct home caution

questions.q: Four people use a mixer grinder. A: dry hands, dry floor, plug top cracked to show bare metal. B: wet hands, dry kitchen, plug intact. C: dry hands, dry kitchen, plug intact. D: dry hands, intact plug, standing in a flooded shed. Whose use follows every caution of the chapter?
o: C only
A and C
C and D
B and C
questions.a: The chapter forbids touching switches or plugs with wet hands (B), using electrical devices in wet areas (D), and handling equipment with damaged insulation or broken plugs (A). Only C breaks none.

questions.q: Rishi's torch runs on cells, while the school's tube light is connected to the wall socket. (a) Which of the two supplies may students use for experiments? (b) Using a property of the human body, say why the other must not be used.
questions.a: (a) Cells or batteries, like those in torchlights. (b) Our body is a conductor of electricity, so current from the power supply passing through it may cause severe injury or even death.
s: Part (a): cells or batteries
Part (b): the body is a conductor, current may cause injury or death

questions.q: Tanvi forgot to remove the plastic covering from the free ends of her tester's wires. (a) What does the lamp do when she presses the covered ends together? (b) Which property of the covering does this show, and why do we want that property on a house wire?
questions.a: (a) The lamp stays dark, because the covering keeps the metal of the wires from touching. (b) The covering is an insulator; on a house wire it protects people from electric shocks.
s: Part (a): lamp stays dark, covering blocks the current
Part (b): insulator, protects people from shocks

questions.q:
During the monsoon in Kochi, Anwar's mother is about to switch on a mixer grinder for dinner. Her hands are wet from washing rice, the kitchen floor is damp, and the plug top has a crack that shows the bare metal under it. She is considering three plans: tape the crack and use the grinder now; call an electrician to replace the plug top (Rs 150, about one hour's wait); or grind the batter by hand on the stone (no cost, about 40 minutes of work).
(a) Which property of the human body makes this situation dangerous?
(b) What material should a plug top be made of, and what has the crack done to its protection?
(c) Which of the three plans does the chapter rule out, and for which reasons?
(d) Choose between the two remaining plans and give a reason for your choice.
questions.a: (a) Our body is a conductor of electricity. (b) An insulator such as plastic or rubber; the crack exposes the bare metal, so the protection is damaged. (c) Taping the crack and using it: the chapter says never to touch plugs with wet hands, never to use electrical devices in wet areas, and never to handle equipment with damaged insulation or broken plugs. (d) A reasoned choice, e.g. hand grinding costs nothing and can start at once but takes effort, while the electrician costs Rs 150 and a wait but mends the plug for later use; either follows the chapter.
s: Part (a): the body is a conductor
Part (b): insulator; the crack exposes bare metal
Part (c): rules out taping and using it, with the cautions
Part (d): a reasoned choice between the two safe plans

questions.q:
Match each part or object (column I) with what it does or shows (column II).
Column I: 1. The pins of a plug that carry current to an appliance  2. The sleeve over a wire  3. The core of house wires, mainly  4. A rubber eraser touched by the free ends of a tester
Column II: a. A conductor, so current passes to the appliance  b. An insulator that protects people from electric shocks  c. Copper, chosen for its comparatively lower cost and abundant supply  d. The lamp stays dark, as current cannot pass through it
questions.a: Plug pins are conductors; the sleeve is an insulator; copper is mainly used for the core for its lower cost and abundant supply; the eraser, a rubber insulator, keeps the tester's lamp dark.

questions.q: A conduction tester has its lamp and cell joined. Predict whether the lamp glows, with a reason, in each case: (i) wire ends touching a steel spoon; (ii) wire ends touching a plastic scale; (iii) wire ends still covered with plastic touching the spoon; (iv) the two free ends touching each other.
questions.a: (i) Glows: steel is a conductor. (ii) Does not glow: plastic is an insulator. (iii) Does not glow: the plastic covering is an insulator and the metal of the wire does not touch the spoon. (iv) Glows: the ends complete the circuit directly.
s: Predictions (i) and (ii) with reasons
Prediction (iii) with reason
Prediction (iv) with reason

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: A plug needs both kinds of material: conductors for its connectors and an insulator for its top.
Statement 2: A rubber sleeve over a copper wire stops the copper from conducting current to the appliance.
Statement 3: The electricity coming to a wall socket from a power plant is Direct Current.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
questions.a: Statement 1 is right. In Statement 2 the sleeve only protects people; the copper inside still conducts. In Statement 3 the wall socket supplies Alternating Current; Direct Current is the type usually from batteries.

questions.q:
Class 7 tested a steel spoon, aluminium foil, a metal key, a wooden block, a rubber eraser and a plastic scale with a conduction tester. The lamp glowed for exactly three of the six objects. Mita is making a plug model for the school exhibition, with connectors and a top.
(a) Which three objects made the lamp glow, and what do they share?
(b) Mita covers the metal key fully with a rubber sleeve and touches the tester's free ends to the two ends of the covered key. What does the lamp do, and why?
(c) A friend suggests making the plug top from the aluminium foil 'since foil is cheap'. What does the tester result tell you about this?
(d) For the connectors she can use foil strips (Rs 2 each, torn after a few uses) or metal keys (Rs 10 each, long lasting). Both pass the tester test; choose one and give the reason that decides it.
questions.a: (a) The steel spoon, aluminium foil and metal key; they are all metals, which are conductors. (b) The lamp stays dark: the rubber covering is an insulator and the current cannot pass through it to the metal. (c) The foil made the lamp glow, so it is a conductor and unsuitable for the plug top, which must be an insulator to protect people from electric shocks. (d) A reasoned choice between two conductors, e.g. keys last longer and so are better for a model shown for many days, foil is cheaper but tears; either is acceptable with a reason, since both conduct.
s: Part (a): the three metals, all conductors
Part (b): lamp dark because rubber is an insulator
Part (c): foil conducts, so unsuitable for the top
Part (d): a reasoned choice between two conductors

questions.q: Maya has a steel spoon with a plastic handle. She touches one free end of her tester to the steel bowl and the other to the far end of the plastic handle, and the lamp stays dark. Her friend says, 'So steel is an insulator.' What should Maya conclude and do?
o: She should touch both free ends to the steel bowl, since the plastic handle blocks the current
The lamp stayed dark, so steel is an insulator and she should record this in her table
Steel and plastic are both conductors, but the cell is too weak to light the lamp
The lamp is faulty, so she should replace the cell and repeat exactly the same touches
questions.a: A plastic handle is an insulator, and in her test the current had to pass through it. The result does not describe steel. Touching both free ends to the steel itself tests the steel.

questions.q: Suppose all the wires in a house were made of metal with no plastic or rubber cover, and all the connectors of its plugs were made of plastic. Give one thing that would go wrong in each case.
questions.a: Without covers the wires would not protect people from electric shocks, since the bare metal conducts. With plastic connectors no current would reach the appliance, because plastic is an insulator.
s: Bare metal wires give shocks, no protection
Plastic connectors would not let the current pass

questions.q: You are given a cell, a lamp, wires and three unknown objects X, Y and Z. Write a plan to decide which are conductors, showing your first step, the care needed, how you record results and what the lamp tells you.
questions.a: Make the tester with a cell and a lamp and leave two wire ends free; first touch the free ends together to check that the lamp glows. Touch the free ends to both ends of each object, making sure the wires do not touch each other. Record whether the lamp glows for each in a table. Glowing shows a conductor and no glow an insulator.
s: Makes the tester and checks it first
Touches both ends of each object with the wire ends apart
Records the results in a table
Glow means conductor
No glow means insulator

questions.q: A wire, a switch and a plug are each made of both conductors and insulators. (a) Which part of each is the conductor? (b) Which part of each is the insulator, and what does it do?
questions.a: (a) The wire: its metal core (copper); the switch: its metal parts that complete the circuit; the plug: its connectors. (b) The wire: its plastic or rubber cover; the switch: its plastic cover; the plug: its top. Each insulator protects people from electric shocks.
s: Part (a): metal core, switch contacts and plug connectors are conductors
Part (b): covers and plug top are insulators that protect people

questions.q: Describe a situation in which a student wrongly concludes that a plastic scale is a conductor using a conduction tester. Explain how the lamp could glow, and give the correct way to do the test.
questions.a: E.g. while touching the scale she lets the two free wire ends touch each other. The current then goes straight through the wires and the lamp glows without passing through the scale. The correct way is to touch the free ends to the two ends of the scale, making sure the wires do not touch each other.
s: A situation that gives a false glow
Explains the current goes through the wires, not the scale
The correct procedure

questions.q: Dev touches the two free ends of his conduction tester together before starting. The lamp stays dark, but he goes on to test a steel spoon, gets a dark lamp, and writes 'insulator'. What should he have done first?
o: Found why the tester itself does not glow, as a dark lamp may be due to the tester
Nothing; a dark lamp for the spoon always means that the object is an insulator
Added a second cell, since the first cell is always too weak to test any metals
Removed the plastic covering from the spoon, since it blocks the current
questions.a: The tester is ready only if the lamp glows when its free ends touch. Dev's tester did not glow, so a dark lamp for the spoon proves nothing; he must first look for the fault in the tester.

questions.q: Sunita says, 'Copper is used for house wires because it is a better conductor than silver or gold.' Is she correct?
questions.a: No. The chapter says silver, copper and gold are the best electrical conductors. Copper is mainly used for wires because of its comparatively lower cost and abundant supply, not because it conducts better than the other two.
s: Verdict: not correct
Silver, copper and gold are all among the best conductors
Copper is chosen for lower cost and abundant supply
